about: What raises a conversation: the reader's nickname, or one of the words they
added beside it. The rule is implemented twice — crates/ircx-core/src/text.rs
decides the badge and what a notification rule is asked about, and
src/store/selectors.ts decides the tint and which span inside the line is
marked. Neither can be derived from the other: the frontend needs the matched
span to draw it, the backend needs the answer before the message is sent.
So both read this file. A case added here fails in whichever language has not
learned it yet, which is the only thing keeping a badge that goes loud and a
line with nothing marked in it from being two different opinions again.
A term is matched on nickname boundaries: the characters either side must be
outside \w and RFC 2812's []\^{}|-. `raises` is true when any term matches.
`hushedCases` is the second rule the same two files share: a sender the
reader hushed never raises them, whatever the line says. A separate array
because it asks who spoke rather than what was said — `hushes` in text.rs
and `isHushed` in selectors.ts are what it holds to.

hushedCases.why: The plain case: a name on the list is hushed
Case folded, because nobody types a service's name the way it registered
A whole name, not a prefix: NickServ_ is somebody else wearing the name
And not a substring of one either
Any of them, not only the first
An empty list hushes nobody, which is what a fresh client holds
Not folded by RFC 1459: both languages must agree, and one has no CASEMAPPING to fold with

cases.why: The plain case, and the one every other line here is a departure from
cases.text: syk: have a look at this

cases.why: A longer name that begins with the nick is not the nick
Case folded, because nobody types a nickname the way it is registered
An away nick is a different name, and the reader is not being addressed by it
A hyphen is a nickname character, so syk-foo is somebody else again
A letter outside ASCII is not a nickname character, so it ends the name
Punctuation either side is a boundary, which is how a nick is usually written
A word raises the same way the nick does
A word inside a longer word is not the word
A word is folded like a nick
The hyphen rule is the nick's rule, applied to a word: this is the cost of one rule rather than two
Any of the words, not the first one
A word at the start of the line has a boundary behind it
A word with regex punctuation in it is a word, not a pattern
And that word does not match what the pattern it looks like would have
No nick and no words raises nothing, which is a session that has not registered yet
